text.p: An upturn in Britain's home decorating market, along with market share gains, helped power a profit recovery at retailer Kingfisher Plc's B&Q stores.
Chief executive Sir Geoffrey Mulcahy said on Wednesday that B&Q's recovery was a combination of improved market, increased market share and a better operational performance.
He said the whole do-it-yourself (DIY) market grew by about four or five percent in the first six months of the year, against a flat market last year.
"B&Q we believe increased its market share in that six months," he said by telephone. B&Q's share of the DIY market increased by about 1.6 percentage points to 17.5 percent.

Mulcahy said the home decorating business had benefited from a revival in the housing market. "There's no doubt there is improved confidence in the general housing market."But he warned against reading too much into revived consumer spending.

"I think that consumer confidence has definitely improved in the first half, but I would be relatively cautious about that because we've been through these times before and consumer confidence is somewhat fickle."
B&Q achieved a near 48 percent increase in profits to 47.0 million stg, from 31.8 million last time.
Mulcahy said B&Q's gross margins stayed about the same, but the market was still pretty competitive. "One is having to fight for business."
The company said in March it planned to squeeze about 20 million stg per year in efficiency savings out of B&Q, but not all in the current year. Mulcahy said the plan was going well.
"We're well on track to achieving that. We're seeing improvements to B&Q's sales by operating the business more efficiently and we're seeing reduction in shrinkage levels."

The group opened two B&Q warehouses in the first half and plans another two in the second. Mulcahy said a refit of the smaller supercentre format stores was going to plan and three new-style supercentres would open in the second half.

He said the group was pleased with the improved performance at its electricals retailer Comet, which saw good like-for-like sales growth of 11.9 percent and stable gross margins. It made a loss of three million stg, down from 8.7 million a year ago.
The improvement came from better availability of merchandise in the stores as well as greater efficiency in running the business, the chief executive said.

Mulcahy was encouraged by Woolworths performance, which returned to profit of 4.6 million stg, after a 900,000 loss last time. "What we have seen is an increase in sales due to the merchandise developments that we have been making, particularly in kitchen and home areas and toys."
The group is still reaping benefits from the installation of computerised ordering systems and also seeing good results from the stores that it is re-designing, he added.
Superdrug, where profits rose by 9.3 percent to 16.4 million stg, benefited from a switch to health and beauty. Mulcahy said current plans to install new pharmacies were on track.
French electricals retailer Darty was doing well in a tough French market. Profits were 42.5 million stg, up from 40.0 million.
Mulcahy said costs throughout the business were under control, but there were some pressures on rental costs.
